summary: The paper studies Mamba's in-context learning on random Markov chains and shows empirically that a single-layer Mamba matches the Bayes/minimax-optimal Laplacian (add-β) smoothing estimator, then provides a constructive representation theorem for first-order chains and an information-theoretic hidden-dimension lower bound scaling as 2^k for order-k chains. Ablations pinpoint the temporal convolution inside the Mamba block as the pivotal ingredient, with corroborating results on a switching-Markov process and WikiText-103. The contribution is well-scoped, the theory-experiment link is unusually tight for this genre of paper, and the identification of convolution's role is a genuinely useful mechanistic insight, though the main representation theorem is limited to first-order chains and the natural-language generality is only lightly probed.
strengths: Clear, non-trivial mechanistic finding: single-layer Mamba tracks the Laplacian estimator on random Markov chains, and the construction in Thm. 1 exposes the specific roles of a_t≈1, the convolution window w≥k+1, and the orthogonality/β-summation structure of the readout — the empirical parameter observations (Figs. 4–5) map onto the constructive proof rather than being a post-hoc rationalization.

The convolution ablation (MambaZero and 'Mamba without convolution' in Fig. 3a, plus the w vs. k relation in Fig. 3b) is a clean, well-designed causal test that isolates convolution from gating and non-linearity.

Thm. 2 gives a matching-in-spirit lower bound (d·p ≥ 2^k(1−3ε)log(1/ε)) that applies to any recurrent architecture of any depth under a pointwise guarantee, and is contrasted usefully against the known linear-in-k transformer construction.
The framing complements the existing Markov-ICL literature for transformers (Edelman et al., Nichani et al.) and is honest about being a Mamba-focused study rather than an architectural bake-off.
The switching-Markov experiment (Sec. 5.1) is a nice non-Markovian stress test that reveals a functional role for a_t (a_t≈0 at switch tokens), tying selectivity to a concrete predictive behavior.

key_concerns.issue: The main representation theorem (Thm. 1) covers only first-order chains with dimensions N=S, d=2S, w=2, while Fig. 1b and the abstract/introduction claim Mamba learns the optimal estimator 'for all Markov orders'. The higher-order case is only supported empirically up to order 4 on binary state spaces, and Thm. 2 in fact suggests the dimension cost is exponential in k — the paper should either prove a higher-order construction or scope the 'all orders' language to what is actually shown.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either extend Thm. 1 to order k with the corresponding 2^k-scaled hidden dimension (matching the lower bound), or rewrite the abstract/intro to say 'for first-order chains theoretically and up to order 4 empirically'. Also state what fails empirically at larger k or S so the reader can judge the scope.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical reporting is thin. Fig. 1 mentions 5 seeds, but ablations (Fig. 3, WikiText perplexities in Table 1, switching-Markov, higher-order results) do not clearly report variance across seeds. The WikiText improvements (30.68→27.55 for Mamba, 29.28→28.67 for transformer at ~14.5 M params) are single-number comparisons and it is not established that the 11% vs. 2% gap is outside seed noise.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report mean±std over ≥3 seeds for every ablation, including Table 1 and Fig. 3a/b. Report a paired significance test or CI for the convolution-vs-no-convolution deltas at each depth, and clarify whether hyperparameters were tuned separately for the with/without-convolution variants.

key_concerns.issue: The 'Beyond Markov / natural language' claim (Sec. 5.2) is weaker than the framing suggests. A single dataset (WikiText-103), a single small size (~14.5 M), and a single depth are used to argue that convolution is important for language too; Table 5 (deferred to appendix) reportedly shows the effect shrinks with depth. This undercuts the generality claim in the introduction.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either soften the language-modeling claim to 'convolution helps small, shallow Mamba/Transformer models on WikiText-103' or add experiments at multiple depths/widths and at least one additional corpus, with error bars, so the trend of decreasing convolution importance with depth can be evaluated on its own terms.

key_concerns.issue: The transformer baseline is not carefully controlled. Fig. 1 compares 1- and 2-layer transformers to 1-layer Mamba, and 'linear attention performs similarly to softmax' is asserted (Fig. 7) but not stress-tested. Since the paper contrasts Mamba favorably with transformers on first-order chains, the transformer configuration (parameter count, positional encoding, tuning budget) matters.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Match parameter counts and tuning budgets between Mamba and transformer baselines, report the sweep used to select each, and specify the positional encoding and attention normalization; ideally also compare a 1-layer transformer with an added convolution (analogous to MambaZero's key ingredient).

key_concerns.issue: Thm. 2 depends on a pointwise ∞-norm approximation guarantee holding almost surely over P and x^t_1; this is a strong condition that in-context learners typically only satisfy in expectation or with high probability. The theorem's practical bite for realistic models is therefore less clear than the presentation suggests.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Discuss how the pointwise guarantee relates to average-loss guarantees, and, if possible, provide a weaker high-probability or expectation version so the lower bound speaks to the models actually trained in Sec. 3–4.

key_concerns.issue: Related-work positioning of the 2^k lower bound vs. transformer results (Rajaraman et al., 2024) is asserted but not contextualized carefully: the transformer bound cited is a construction, not a matching lower bound, so the claim that transformers 'need' only linear-in-k dimension is one-sided.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Clarify that the comparison is construction-vs-construction, and note the absence (or presence) of a matching lower bound for transformers, so the Mamba-vs-transformer complexity contrast is not overstated.

key_concerns.issue: Clarity: several equations (the Mamba recurrence block, Eq. (4)–(5), the Input-selectivity block) are dense and, in the current typesetting, hard to parse — e.g. the meaning of tilde-x_t vs. x_t, the exact role of Δ_t, and which quantities are scalars vs. matrices. The construction's readability depends on this.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a schematic that maps each learned parameter block onto the role it plays in the counting estimator (which term produces n_{ij}, which produces β, which enforces the i=x_t gating), and a short worked example on S=2, k=1.

questions_for_authors: Can Thm. 1 be extended to order-k chains with hidden dimension Θ(2^k), matching the lower bound in Thm. 2? If not, what is the obstacle?

Table 1 shows an 11% relative perplexity drop from removing convolution in Mamba vs. only 2% in Transformer at ~14.5 M parameters. What is the seed variance for these numbers, and does the gap survive at multiple depths and parameter budgets beyond what is in the appendix?
In Thm. 2, how sensitive is the 2^k bound to relaxing the pointwise ∞-norm guarantee to an average or high-probability guarantee that better matches the trained models?
For the switching-Markov experiment, does the learned a_t ≈ 0 at switch tokens generalize to variable p_switch, or was it trained and tested at a single value (0.01)?
Is the empirical finding that b_{(ij)}c_t ≈ 0 when i≠x_t (Fig. 5) robust across seeds, initializations, and β values, or only observed in the specific runs shown?

How does the 1-layer Mamba result compare against a 1-layer transformer augmented with an equivalent input convolution — i.e. is convolution alone (independent of the SSM recurrence) sufficient for the counting-estimator behavior on first-order chains?
calibration_check: Claims are mostly scoped to the evidence — the theory is stated for first-order chains and the lower bound is qualified — but the abstract and Sec. 3 language ('learns the optimal estimator for all Markov orders', 'generality on non-Markovian data', natural-language claims) is broader than the experiments and theorems actually justify and should be tightened.

significance.justification: A useful, specific mechanistic result for Mamba's ICL and a clean identification of convolution's role that will interest the growing SSM-mechanism community, but the setting (random Markov chains, small models) limits the immediate practical impact.

novelty.justification: First application of the Markov-ICL framework to Mamba, first constructive proof that a Mamba-like SSM realizes the add-β estimator, and first 2^k hidden-dimension lower bound for recurrent architectures on this task.

rigor.justification: The Thm. 1 construction is tightly coupled to observable model quantities (a_t≈1, b_{(ij)}c_t≈0, w=k+1), and Thm. 2 is a nontrivial information-theoretic argument, though the pointwise guarantee is a strong assumption and the higher-order case is left empirical.

statistical_soundness.justification: Fig. 1 reports 5-seed error bars, but Fig. 3 ablations, Table 1 perplexities, and higher-order/switching experiments lack visible variance estimates or significance tests, making the size of key effects hard to certify.

calibration_honesty.justification: Limitations (representation-only scope, first-order theory, depth-1 focus) are acknowledged, but 'all Markov orders' and 'generality' language in the abstract/intro overshoots the actual first-order theorem and modest NL experiments.

clarity.justification: Structure is clean and the core intuition (convolution provides the length-k prefix, recurrence accumulates counts, readout enforces β-smoothing) is well conveyed, but the equation-heavy Mamba block and Eqs. (4)–(5) are hard to parse without more careful typesetting and a worked example.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard Intro / Related / Setup / Empirical / Theory / Extensions / Conclusion layout, appropriate length, and reasonable use of the appendix.

reproducibility.justification: Data generation, loss, optimizer, and architectural parameters (N, d, e, w) are specified; however many hyperparameters, seed counts for ablations, and language-modeling training details are pushed to appendices whose content cannot be fully assessed from the main text.

related_work.justification: Relevant prior work on Markov-ICL for transformers, Mamba/SSM expressivity, and ICL empirics is discussed, but the Mamba-vs-Transformer complexity comparison is one-sided (construction vs. construction, no matching lower bound cited) and could be positioned more evenhandedly.

figure_quality.justification: Captions describe informative figures — next-token probability trajectories, L1 deviation vs. Markov order, ablation curves, convolution-window vs. order — that directly support the claims, though the mapping between the construction's parameter structures and the plotted quantities could be tightened.

breadth_generality.justification: Theory is first-order-only; empirical Markov results go up to order 4 and small state spaces; the language-modeling section relies on one dataset at one scale, so the claimed generality is under-supported.

overall_recommendation.justification: A borderline-accept paper: a clear, well-executed mechanistic study with a tight theory-experiment loop and a genuinely interesting lower bound, held back by first-order-only theory, thin variance reporting on ablations, and lightweight generality experiments.
